          COMES NOW the Office of the Public Counsel and for its Initial Brief states:

                                                    Introduction

         Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro’s (“EMM”) rates from its last rate case

are just and reasonable until the Commission determines that they are not. 1 Because it is seeking

a rate increase EMM has the burden of showing that its current rates no longer are just and

reasonable. 2 Public Counsel’s primary issues in this case are whether, or how, the Commission

allows EMM to recover from Missourians through rates its investment, costs, and expenses related

to Mullin Creek #2 (Issue 20.B.); what return-on-equity the Commission authorizes (Issue 1.C.);

what EMM capital structure the Commission authorizes (Issue 1.A.); what income tax impact the

Commission recognizes for losses EMM has incurred when it disposed of assets (Issue 15.A.i.);

and what of EMM’s investments in distribution and transmission projects since its last rate case

the Commission allows EMM to recover from Missourians through rates (Issues 18.B., 19.A.&B.,

& 20.F.&H.).

         Nothing in any of the various stipulations and agreements different parties filed in this case

limits the Commission. Not only is the Commission free to independently decide each issue

limited only in that its decisions must be supported by the record before the Commission, not

arbitrary or capricious, and lawful, that is the role and obligation for which the Legislature

authorized it.

            The evidentiary hearing record in this case closed on October 13, 2026. This brief is due

                                                    Argument

      1. Cost of Capital
      A. What is the appropriate capital structure to use for ratemaking in this proceeding?
          Public Counsel’s Position: The 45% common equity and 55% long-term debt
      ratemaking capital structure which Public Counsel witness David Murray determined is
      consistent with Evergy, Inc.’s more cost efficient targeted and average quarterly capital
      structure ratios for the period June 30, 2024, through June 30, 2026. Evergy Metro, Inc. is
      a subsidiary in a holding company structure where Evergy, Inc. is the ultimate parent.
      Evergy, Inc. issues equity and long-term debt in the capital markets through arms-length
      transactions with third parties. While Evergy Metro, Inc. does issue its own debt, its capital
      structure is managed through internal capital flows to achieve a common equity ratio of 52%
      at a specific point-in-time for ratemaking, which is the true-up date of June 30, 2026. By
      manipulating Evergy Metro Inc.’s common equity ratio to a suboptimal 52% common
      equity ratio Evergy is requesting the Commission to have Evergy Metro Inc.’s Missouri
      customers pay for a higher-cost capital structure than the capital structure which it targets
      for itself, despite the fact that legislative and regulatory changes in Missouri have shifted
      business risk from investors to ratepayers. Evergy Metro, Inc.’s Missouri ratepayers
      deserve credit for this shift in risk by being charged a rate-of-return that is consistent with
      Evergy, Inc.’s market-based capital structure ratios, ratios which Evergy, Inc. has
      dynamically managed to take advantage of its reduced business risk that flows to it from its
      regulated utility subsidiaries. 3


Public Counsel’s Argument: As Public Counsel witness David Murray explains, EMM’s parent,

Evergy, Inc. (“Evergy”), targets the capital structures of Evergy and its subsidiaries as a


3

                                                          5
 consolidated group to optimize the cost of capital funds from the debt and equity markets for the

benefit of Evergy’s shareholders. Because, as a wholly owned subsidiary of Evergy, EMM does

not directly access the equity markets, Evergy and EMM control EMM’s capital structure by

controlling the capital flows between EMM and Evergy through dividend payments or non-

payments. If Evergy does not require EMM and its affiliate subsidiaries to provide sufficient

dividends to fund dividends to Evergy’s third-party shareholders, Evergy issues holding company

debt capital to fund the deficiency. Evergy’s capacity to do so is based on EMM’s and its affiliate

subsidiaries’ low-risk regulated utility operations. Evergy and EMM exercise their collective

control to maximize Evergy’s shareholders’ wealth—since equity receives a higher return than

debt, and applying this higher return to a higher common equity ratio achieves an even higher

return to the lower consolidated common equity ratio in Evergy’s consolidated capital structure.

Based on his analysis of Evergy consolidated group’s targeted and average quarterly capital

structure ratios for the period June 30, 2024, through June 30, 2026, and the fact that Evergy’s

primary assets are regulated utilities, including EMM, a capital structure of 45.00% common

equity and 55.00% long-term debt represents a more reasonable capital structure for Evergy’s

subsidiary EMM than EMM’s manipulated actual capital structure of 52.19% common equity and

47.18% long-term debt. 4 It is particularly disturbing that EMM is targeting such an equity rich

capital structure when Missouri’s more investor-friendly legislative and regulatory environment

has allowed Evergy to utilize more debt capacity—lowering its common equity ratio—while still

maintaining the same credit rating. The Commission is the only entity that has the authority to

ensure EMM’s Missouri retail customers are not charged for a more expensive capital structure




4
 Ex. 205, Public Counsel witness David Murray direct testimony; Ex. 207, Public Counsel witness David Murray
surrebuttal and true-up direct testimony, Sch. DM-S-2.

                                                      6
 than the 45% common equity and 55% long-term debt capital structure ratios Evergy truly

considers to be more cost efficient.

           That Evergy and EMM are targeting a 52% common equity and 48% long-term debt capital

structure for EMM is demonstrated by the common equity ratios of Evergy’s subsidiaries EMM

and Evergy Missouri West (“EMW”) in their Missouri rate cases since 2022. Likewise, Union

Electric Company d/b/a Ameren Missouri also has targeted that same capital structure ratio in its

rate cases for approximately the past decade. All have done so despite Missouri making legislative

and regulatory changes during the past decade which have shifted business risk from investors to

ratepayers and despite rating agencies recognizing those business risk reductions when rating the

holding companies—Evergy and Ameren—which allows them to issue more debt without

lowering their credit ratings. 5

           Moody’s Ratings has relaxed its credit metric thresholds for the holding companies, but

not the Missouri subsidiaries of the holding companies. This is because Ameren and Evergy are

bargaining with Moody’s Ratings over credit ratings on behalf of their consolidated holding

company groups, not specifically for the individual subsidiaries that have realized the lower

business risk. 6 Before the Commission authorized Union Electric Company and Kansas City

Power & Light Company (now EMM) to reorganize and become wholly-owned subsidiaries, there

was only one possible capital structure to evaluate for making their rates—their capital structure.

That meant that if Union Electric Company or Kansas City Power & Light Company increased

their leverage during a construction cycle by issuing more debt than equity, that leverage was

captured in their authorized RORs.                 The Commission can correct Evergy and EMM’s

6

 misallocation of lower costs of capital to shareholders at the expense of EMM’s retail customers

by at least considering the contradiction between the capital structures of EMM and the Evergy

consolidated group. Public Counsel consistently has been addressing this issue for many years.

But now the discrepancy between equity-rich subsidiary capital structures and more leveraged

(equity poorer) capital structures of consolidated utility groups has captured broader national

scrutiny recently in other jurisdictions due to an increased focus on affordability issues.

           Troubling to Public Counsel is that Evergy characterizes Public Counsel’s position to be

extraordinary.       Evergy used the same strategy when it attempted to discredit the Kansas

Corporation Commission’s (“KCC”) Staff’s recommendation to consider holding company debt

when setting rates for Evergy’s Kansas subsidiaries. For purposes of Evergy’s Capital Structure

& Return on Equity Policy Workshop (“Workshop”) before the KCC, Evergy reviewed 109 rate

cases and claimed that “[i]n none of those cases did we observe any evidence of holding company

debt being attributed to subsidiary utilities in the final rate decisions.” 7 In that Workshop, Evergy

was attempting to discredit the KCC Staff’s methodology of specifically allocating holding

company debt to Evergy’s utility subsidiaries operating in Kansas, Evergy Kansas Central and

Evergy Metro d/b/a Evergy Kansas Metro. However, Evergy did not include the fact that many

jurisdictions do consider the discrepancy between the capital structures of the holding company

consolidated group and that of the regulated utility subsidiary being reviewed when deciding a fair

and reasonable ratemaking capital structure for that subsidiary. Based on his experience and past

research, Mr. Murray was aware that both the KCC and the Illinois Commerce Commission

(“ICC”) consider the capital structures of the holding company consolidated group when




7
    Ex. 50, EMM witness Geoffrey Ley rebuttal testimony, pp. 5-6.

                                                         8
 determining a fair and reasonable authorized ROR for the subsidiary in question. 8 Additionally,

after Mr. Murray reviewed EMM’s workpapers from the 109 rate case decisions Mr. Ley testified

supported not allocating Evergy’s holding company debt to its subsidiaries, Mr. Murray discovered

that several other utility commissions also consider the more leveraged parent company and proxy

group’s capital structures when deciding a fair and reasonable ratemaking capital structure. Those

utility commissions are the Arkansas, Indiana, Louisianna, New York, and Oklahoma

commissions. 9

        Not until Great Plains Energy (“GPE”) and Westar Inc. merged to form Evergy did a fair

and reasonable capital structure became a disputed issue in EMM and Evergy Missouri West’s

Missouri rate cases. GPE (EMM’s ultimate parent before the Westar merger) did not leverage its

equity investments in its subsidiaries—EMM and EMW. Therefore, GPE’s capital structure was

similar to that of its subsidiaries. Before the Westar merger use of GPE’s consolidated capital

structure in Missouri for purposes of setting a ROR for EMM and EMW for ratemaking was not

controversial. Under the GPE holding company umbrella, Metro and EMW distributed sufficient

dividends to GPE to allow it to fund dividends to third-party shareholders Essentially, GPE was

a pass-through company that did not issue long-term holding company debt or hybrid securities,

unless it did so on behalf of EMW before it regained its credit standing. This paradigm changed

with the creation of Evergy, which now causes its subsidiaries’ capital structures to be more

financially interconnected. As EMM witness Mr. Ley admitted during Evergy’s presentation to

the KCC, Evergy issues holding company capital to fund dividends to third party shareholders.10

While this financial strategy is efficient for the Evergy enterprise, it demonstrates the

years, Elliott Investment Management L.P. (“Elliott”) took a sizeable position in Evergy’s

outstanding common equity then initiated a change in Evergy’s financial and investment

strategy. 12 As a result of Elliott’s initiative Evergy discontinued using holding company debt to

fund its stock buyback program and began using it to support Evergy’s ramped up spending in

utility infrastructure, with specific emphasis on investing in Missouri due to the additional

shareholder value PISA permitted. 13

        Through discovery Mr. Murray found corporate records which specifically confirmed that

Evergy’s new increases in investment should create even more shareholder wealth if they are

supported by higher leverage (higher debt-to-equity) at the holding company level. 14 As Mr.

Murray testifies, Evergy’s financial strategy to increase shareholder wealth requires optimizing

the consolidated group capital structure to achieve a lower cost of capital for the group, but not for

the subsidiaries. If Evergy optimized its subsidiaries’ capital structures and these lower cost capital

structures were reflected in the rates charged to the retail customers of those subsidiaries, then

Evergy could not maximize its shareholders’ wealth through the increased rate revenues it would

 get with rates made based on suboptimal less leveraged capital structures. It is Evergy’s conflict

of interest of desiring higher common equity ratios at its subsidiaries to support higher revenue

requirements at the same time Evergy is attempting to minimize the cost of capital at the

consolidated group level which requires the Commission to protect the public by setting EMM’s

rate-of-return based on capital structure ratios more consistent with Evergy’s more cost-efficient

consolidated group capital structure.

       When deciding a fair and reasonable ratemaking capital structure the Commission should also

consider the logic underlying the Commission’s affiliate transaction rules. Effectively, by using

more leverage in its consolidated group capital structure than at its subsidiaries, Evergy is

admitting that it can achieve a lower market cost of capital than what it charges EMM for capital.

The Commission’s affiliate transaction rules require unregulated affiliates to charge regulated

utilities the lower of cost or market value. With how Evergy is managing the capital structures of

its consolidated group and its subsidiaries, Evergy is not only charging EMM more than a

reasonable market cost of capital, it is also charging EMM for a rate-of-return that is higher than

what it would be based on Evergy’s consolidated group’s cost of equity and embedded cost of

debt. This leads to Public Counsel’s position about a fair and reasonable return-on-equity to apply

to EMM’s rate base to be charged to EMM’s retail customers in Missouri.

       B. What cost of debt should be used for determining rate of return?
          Public Counsel’s Position: 4.54% based on Evergy Missouri Metro’s embedded cost of
       long-term debt as of June 30, 2026. 15

 Public Counsel’s Argument: Because this is EMM’s actual cost of long-term debt based on a

weighted average of EMM’s long-term debt portfolio as of the end of the true-up period (June 30,

2026), this debt rate is undisputed.

     C. What return on common equity should be used for determining rate of return?
        Public Counsel’s Position: 9.25%, the midpoint of Mr. Murray’s recommended
     authorized ROE range of 9.00% to 9.50%, a range which is based on the following
     considerations:
       • The electric utility industry’s cost of equity (“COE”) in 2015 was very similar to the
         current COE when this Commission authorized a 9.50% ROE for Evergy Missouri
         Metro;
       • Mr. Murray’s recommended 9.25% ROE fairly balances Every Missouri Metro’s
         shareholder compensation with the ratepayer burdens that Every Missouri Metro’s
         planned significant capital investments will create;
       • Every Missouri Metro will create additional shareholder wealth if it earns a ROE above
         its approximately 8.00% COE; and
       • 9.25% is reasonable under the Commission’s zone of reasonableness standard of 100
         basis points above and below recently authorized ROEs—here 9.70%, for a zone of
         reasonableness of 8.70% to 10.70%. 16


Public Counsel’s Argument: As Public Counsel stated in its position statement for this issue

(see immediately above), the return-on-equity (“ROE”) the Commission should allow for

designing EMM’s rates is 9.25% based on Mr. Murray’s analysis showing that a return-on-equity

range of 9.0% to 9.5% with a midpoint of 9.25% is reasonable. 17 While the allowed ROE Mr.

Murray recommends is less than the ROE of 9.5% the Commission last explicitly allowed for

EMM in EMM’s 2015 general electric rate case, Mr. Murray provided evidence which shows that,

due to EMM’s increased scale of investment over the next few years and his estimate that EMM’s

COE is 8%, EMM will be able to create a disproportionate amount of shareholder wealth. 18

         Public Counsel witness David Murray performed a COE analysis on a broad proxy group

of electric utility companies, which included Evergy Inc., but he gave more weight to certain

subsets of that group which include companies which are more concentrated in vertically

integrated regulated electric utility operations. 19 Mr. Murray applied two primary methodologies,

a discounted cash flow (“DCF”) method and the Capital Asset Pricing Model (“CAPM”),

commonly used by investors to estimate the COE of and fair values for utility stocks. Mr. Murray

applied the multi-stage version of the DCF to his electric utility proxy group because he determined

utility industry equity investment analysts use this version. Mr. Murray’s DCF analysis explicitly

emphasized “equity analysts’ consensus estimated dividends and the modeled growth of

dividends.” “When the DCF method is applied to dividends as the proxy for cash flow, it is more

specifically defined as the dividend discount model (“DDM”).” 20

        Mr. Murray used equity analysts’ discrete annual dividends per share (“DPS”) estimates

for the first stage of his DDM analysis, then he estimated the transitionary growth rate in DPS for

each company during the second stage in order for all companies to achieve a perpetual DPS

growth rate in the final stage. 21 This ensures the assumptions of sustainable growth are met, which

are a constant dividend payout ratio (DPS/EPS) with dividends, earnings and book value growing

at the same rate. 22 Mr. Murray’s approach and assumptions are similar to those that equity

investment analysts actually use and, thus, upon what investors actually rely. 23         As Murray

testified, “My analysis has allowed me to test the theory of cost of capital estimation in utility ROR

testimony, as it compares to practice.” 24 Mr. Murray’s study resulted in an estimated COE of

        Staff arrived at COE estimates for EMM of 7.11% to 10.34% using a DCF method and the

CAPM. 31 However, Staff recommended a ROE of 9.73% (range of 9.72% to 9.74%) based on

rate case in 2024, Dr. Won recommends essentially the same ROE. 33 Dr. Won’s lack of adjustment

the Bluefield decision, which is that “A rate of return may be reasonable at one time, and become

too high or too low by changes affecting opportunities for investment, the money market, and

        In contrast to both Staff’s and Public Counsel’s witnesses, EMM’s ROR witness, Ann E.

a utility’s authorized ROE at parity with the COE is consistent with the Hope and Bluefield

methodology she labeled as a Bond Yield Plus Risk Premium (“BYPRP”) methodology – all of

which she applied to her electric utility proxy group. 37
